summary: Compares two proposals for supporting IPv6 in the DNS, the A6 approach and the AAAA approach, and examines the pros and cons of each. It was written to clarify a debate that had not reached consensus, so the IETF could reach closure. It updates RFCs 2673 and 2874.

plainLanguage.summary: Two groups wanted to store new internet addresses in different ways and could not agree. This note lays out the strengths and weaknesses of each so people can decide.

questions: what are the tradeoffs for ipv6 dns support
what is a dns bit label
subtitle: A side-by-side look at two competing ways to store IPv6 addresses in the DNS, and when each one makes sense.

tldr.problem: The IETF had two Proposed Standards for putting IPv6 addresses in the DNS, AAAA and A6, and had not reached consensus on which to prefer.
tldr.mechanism: The note weighs each approach on read cost, write cost, DNSSEC, dynamic update, transition and the reverse mapping tree, then ties the choice to one question: will IPv6 do rapid renumbering or GSE-like routing?
tldr.outcome: If yes, move to A6 and DNAME. If no, keep the simpler AAAA record. Either way, use the textual form for the reverse tree, not bit labels.

facts.label: Reverse tree fan-out
facts.value: At most 16 NS RRsets per label level

today: RFC 3364 is an Informational note that updates RFC 2673 and RFC 2874, and no later RFC is recorded as updating or obsoleting it. It does not specify a standard; it lays out the tradeoffs and recommendations as of August 2002.

sections.title: Two Proposals on the Table
sections.content:
RFC 1886 defined a straightforward way to store IPv6 addresses in the DNS. It closely resembles how IPv4 is handled, with a small improvement to reverse mapping based on experience with CIDR. RFC 2874 defined enhanced mechanisms that let an IPv6 address be split across several DNS resource records, so the data can follow the network topology behind the address. Both were Proposed Standards and both came from the IPNG Working Group.

Both have been implemented, though RFC 1886 is more widespread because it is older and simpler. The open questions are whether the more general mechanism is really needed, what new usage problems it brings, and how it affects IPv6 deployment. The one point of wide agreement is that the decision should be made soon.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to write an address in the big phone book of the internet. People have used the simple way longer, and the fancy way can do more tricks. This note asks which one we really need.

sections.title: AAAA Versus A6: What Each Is Good At
sections.content:
The A6 record from RFC 2874 is a superset of the AAAA record from RFC 1886. Its unique strength is that a prefix portion of an address can change without any action by whoever controls the zone holding the least significant bits. That covers "rapid renumbering" and routing schemes such as the former GSE proposal. A6 still does not remove every zone update during renumbering: changing ISPs would usually need a change to the upward delegation pointer.

Many A6 features can be imitated with AAAA records by preprocessing zone files. But the preprocessor needs exactly the information A6 stores in the DNS, so it has to get it from somewhere. Also, A6 with a zero-length prefix ("A6 0") is semantically equivalent to AAAA, with one wasted octet on the wire.

AAAA has two selling points. It is essentially identical to IPv4's A record apart from length, so there are more than 15 years of experience with its usage patterns and failure modes. And it is "optimized for read": a complete address is fetched in one piece, at the expense of more effort when injecting new data. A6 is the reverse, "optimized for write".

The RFC calls some arguments less compelling. That A6 maps zone files to topology is an argument for better zone tools, not for changing the wire protocol. That AAAA is more widely deployed is weak, since transition tools can be built. That A6 allows more broken configurations is also an argument for better tools.
sections.plainLanguage: The simple way keeps the whole address in one place, so looking it up is fast. The fancy way keeps it in pieces, so changing part of it is easy but putting it together takes more steps.

sections.title: Potential Problems with A6
sections.content:
The main concern is chaining. Resolving an N-link chain of A6 records involves a series of almost independent queries. If one AAAA lookup takes time T, the note guesses a chain takes something approaching N*T, softened by caching of the fragments for the more significant bits. A resolver then has two poor choices: shorten the wait per fragment or lengthen the total wait before failing. Users are already impatient with IPv4 lookups, so indiscriminate use of long A6 chains is likely to cause problems. Assuming each query fails independently, the failure probability would also be roughly proportional to N.

A6 prefix names often point out of the zone and to another organization, such as an ISP. The RFC notes that experience with glue records and PTR records in IN-ADDR.ARPA suggests many administrators do not maintain such pointers well. The AAAA preprocessing alternative has many of the same problems.

One past worry turns out not to be serious. An A6 chain can branch into a tree, which critics feared would cause a query explosion. A resolver that follows the "bounded work per query" rule from RFC 1034 limits work for a simple query, a CNAME chain, an A6 tree or a loop alike.
sections.plainLanguage: Building an address from pieces is like a treasure hunt with clues held by different people. The more clues, the longer it takes and the more chances something goes wrong.

sections.title: DNSSEC, Dynamic Update and Transition
sections.content:
Re-signing after renumbering takes longer with AAAA, because every address record is re-signed, than with A6, where a common prefix record and a few A6 0 records are re-signed. This is not a serious scaling problem since re-signing happens in leaf zones. Against that, validating A6 needs more work because each fragment has its own signature, and a message with many fragments and signatures is larger than one with a single AAAA and one signature.

As a data point, private testing by Bill Sommerfeld found a 333MHz Celeron laptop could generate roughly 40 1024-bit RSA signatures per second. The RFC extrapolates a few hours to sign a zone of 105 hosts and about a day for 106 hosts using AAAA. Re-signing is only likely to be prohibitive in the rapid renumbering case where AAAA does not work well anyway.

Dynamic update works about equally for both, except that an A6 update client needs the prefix length and prefix name. No mechanism informs clients of these yet; the RFC suggests a DHCP extension.

Moving from AAAA to A6 is possible through AAAA synthesis: a resolver doing iterative resolution for a client synthesizes AAAA records from equivalent A6 queries. A DNSSEC signature cannot be generated for such a synthesized record, so clients that validate for themselves must issue A6 queries directly.
sections.plainLanguage: Stamping every address with a security seal takes longer when there are many whole addresses. But checking seals is slower when each piece of an address has its own seal.

sections.title: Reverse Mapping: Text Labels, Bit Labels and DNAME
sections.content:
The IPv6 reverse tree is the counterpart of IPv4's IN-ADDR.ARPA. RFC 1886 uses the hexadecimal form of the address, reversed, with a dot between each hex digit and a well-known suffix. Names are tedious for people but easy for programs, and delegation on arbitrary bit boundaries gives at most 16 NS RRsets per label level. The weak spot is delegation in the least significant label, but there seems to be no real need to delegate the least significant four bits.

RFC 2874 proposed a new bit label type that writes binary addresses directly, which is much more compact. But deploying a new DNS label type is very hard: every authoritative server for the name and every resolver involved must be upgraded, and servers that are not upgraded reject the query as malformed. The note concludes the textual form is good enough.

RFC 2874 also proposed DNAME records in the reverse tree to give the same fragmenting power that A6 gives the main tree. The need for DNAME is therefore tied to the need for fragmented A6: if one is needed, so is the other.
sections.plainLanguage: Looking up a name from an address is like finding a street by its number. Writing the number out digit by digit is long but every phone can read it. A new compact code would need every phone updated first.

sections.title: The Recommendation
sections.content:
The note boils the debate down to two questions: will IPv6 do rapid renumbering or GSE-like routing, and will the reverse tree need delegation in the least significant four bits? The first is the key and is a decision for the IPv6 community, not the DNS community. The second is fairly obviously "no".

  • If the IPv6 working groups seriously intend rapid renumbering or GSE-like routing, transition to A6 in the main tree and use DNAME as needed in the reverse tree.
  • Otherwise, keep the simpler AAAA solution and do not use DNAME in the reverse tree.
  • In either case, the reverse tree should use the textual form from RFC 1886, not bit labels.
  • If A6 and DNAME are adopted, write applicability statements and implementation guidelines to discourage excessively complex use. Anything that can be described with A6 0 records and without DNAME should be.

On security, the note says the two mechanisms have similar characteristics, with differing DNSSEC interactions and added operational and protocol complexity in RFC 2874. There are no IANA actions, since the record types were already allocated.
sections.plainLanguage: The advice is: only use the fancy way if you truly need to change addresses in a hurry. If not, stick with the simple one, and always use the readable style for looking up names from addresses.
